triage.name: Diverticulosis and Diverticulitis
triage.reason: Left lower quadrant pain with fever and a clear CT-based diagnosis; strong acute abdomen differential including colitis and malignancy.

demographics: More common with older age; under 50 slightly more common in men, after 60 slightly more common in women.

chief_complaints.text: I have severe pain in my lower left belly
I feel sick to my stomach

hpi.onset: Acute, often over several hours; less commonly subacute over 2–3 days.
hpi.duration: Most patients seek care within 1–3 days of symptom onset.
hpi.progression: Pain typically starts in the left lower quadrant and becomes constant. If inflammation worsens, fever and gastrointestinal symptoms may appear.
hpi.location: Left lower quadrant; may be suprapubic or straddle the midline if the sigmoid colon is redundant.
hpi.quality: Constant, aching or crampy; may be sharp if peritoneal inflammation is intense.
hpi.timing: Constant and may worsen with movement, coughing, or pressure.
pertinent_negatives: Vomiting that started before the pain
Urinary symptoms as the main complaint

positives.text: Abdominal pain in the left lower quadrant

argues_against: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
Sudden one-sided pelvic pain with vomiting

atypical.how_it_differs: May have less prominent fever and pain; presentation can be vague with only confusion, malaise, or ileus.
Symptoms can be subtle or rapidly progressive with severe sepsis; localizing signs may be reduced.
Rare, but when it occurs the gravid uterus can displace the sigmoid colon so pain may be higher or on the right.

general.mild: Uncomfortable but not toxic; may be mildly febrile
general.moderate: Lies still, avoids moving, febrile, localized left lower quadrant pain
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale, diaphoretic, hypotensive, may have diffuse peritonitis

findings.term: Tenderness of left lower quadrant of abdomen

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to cough or gently percuss the abdomen
findings.finding: Pain with jarring, suggesting peritoneal irritation

findings.maneuver: Auscultate all four quadrants for 2 minutes
Deeply palpate the left lower quadrant

findings.term: Tenderness of right lower quadrant of abdomen

findings.maneuver: Pelvic exam when a gynecologic cause is possible
findings.finding: No cervical motion tenderness or adnexal tenderness

labs.caveat: A normal white count does not rule out diverticulitis, especially in mild disease or older adults.
Rises after 6-12 hours; higher values suggest complication.
Sterile pyuria from inflammation adjacent to the bladder; can mislead toward a urinary infection.
Negative. Required before ionizing radiation in anyone who could be pregnant; rules out ectopic pregnancy.

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Nonpregnant adults; recommended first-line imaging for suspected acute diverticulitis

findings.text: Focal sigmoid wall thickening greater than 5 mm
Small amount of free fluid near the sigmoid colon

imaging.preferred_when: Pregnant patients or children, to avoid radiation

findings.text: Thickened hypoechoic segment of sigmoid colon
Inflamed diverticulum with surrounding echogenic fat
Fluid collection or abscess adjacent to the colon

imaging.study: MRI abdomen and pelvis without contrast

findings.text: Segmental colonic wall thickening with pericolonic inflammation
Nonspecific bowel gas pattern or mild ileus

imaging.preferred_when: After the acute episode, to rule out colorectal cancer in selected patients

findings.text: Diverticula throughout the colon, predominantly sigmoid
Erythema or edema around an inflamed diverticulum

initial.why: Leukocytosis with left shift supports an inflammatory process
Assess dehydration, electrolytes, and renal function before IV contrast and treatment
Check for urinary infection or stone that can mimic diverticulitis; sterile pyuria can occur

confirmatory.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
confirmatory.why: Most accurate test for acute diverticulitis and its complications

supporting.why: Inflammatory marker; elevated in diverticulitis and may suggest abscess or perforation
Avoids radiation; can show inflamed diverticulum

supporting.test: MRI abdomen and pelvis without contrast
supporting.why: Avoids radiation; alternative if CT contraindicated

not_indicated.why: Nonspecific; CT is preferred when imaging is needed
Contraindicated during acute diverticulitis due to perforation risk; may be done after recovery to exclude cancer
No role in evaluating abdominal pain
Not indicated unless epigastric pain or pancreatitis suspected

decision_points: Perform pregnancy test before CT in anyone who could be pregnant
CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast is the preferred imaging study in nonpregnant adults
Avoid colonoscopy during acute diverticulitis due to risk of perforation
In pregnant patients, start with ultrasound and use MRI if needed

differential.name: Colorectal cancer
differential.why_considered: Left lower quadrant pain and change in bowel habits in an older adult; can mimic or complicate diverticulitis, especially if a mass or stricture is present.
differential.trigger: Unintentional weight loss, iron deficiency anemia, or change in stool caliber in a patient over 50

history: Change in bowel habits over weeks to months
imaging: Irregular focal mass or stricture with shouldering on CT
Colonoscopy after resolution of acute inflammation shows malignancy

differential.name: Irritable bowel syndrome
differential.why_considered: Recurrent lower abdominal pain with bloating, constipation, or diarrhea; chronic symptoms may be mistaken for smoldering diverticular disease.

history: Chronic or recurrent pain over months, often related to defecation
exam: Normal abdominal exam, no localized tenderness
imaging: CT or colonoscopy normal or only uncomplicated diverticula, no acute inflammation

differential.name: Appendicitis
differential.why_considered: Acute lower abdominal pain, fever, and leukocytosis; can be confused with diverticulitis, especially if pain is not clearly left-sided.
differential.trigger: Periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant or right lower quadrant tenderness

history: Pain begins periumbilically then migrates to right lower quadrant
imaging: CT shows enlarged appendix with surrounding inflammation, normal sigmoid

differential.name: Ectopic pregnancy
differential.why_considered: Lower abdominal pain in a person who could be pregnant; can mimic diverticulitis if pain is left-sided.
differential.trigger: Positive pregnancy test or any person of childbearing age with abdominal pain

exam: Signs of hemodynamic instability if ruptured
imaging: No intrauterine pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound

differential.name: Urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis
differential.why_considered: Lower abdominal or pelvic pain with fever and urinary symptoms; diverticulitis can cause sterile pyuria and be mistaken for UTI.

history: Flank pain and chills if pyelonephritis
exam: No localized left lower quadrant peritoneal signs
imaging: CT may show normal colon or only bladder wall thickening; if pyelonephritis, kidney findings

differential.name: Kidney stone
differential.why_considered: Left-sided abdominal or pelvic pain with nausea; pain can radiate to groin and be severe.

history: Colicky left flank pain radiating to groin
imaging: Stone and hydronephrosis on CT; normal colon

differential.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
differential.why_considered: Acute or chronic abdominal pain, diarrhea, and fever; CT may show colonic inflammation.

exam: Tenderness may be diffuse or localized; perianal disease in Crohn's
imaging: CT shows skip lesions, terminal ileal thickening, or pancolitis rather than focal sigmoid diverticulitis

differential.name: Ischemic colitis
differential.why_considered: Older adult with left-sided abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea; often has vascular risk factors.

exam: Tenderness may be out of proportion to exam
imaging: CT shows segmental colonic wall thickening, often at splenic flexure

severity.mild: Uncomplicated acute diverticulitis: localized left lower quadrant tenderness, low-grade or no fever, normal to mildly elevated white count; patient is well enough for outpatient management.
severity.moderate: Uncomplicated but more symptomatic: fever, guarding, moderate leukocytosis and CRP elevation; often requires IV antibiotics and bowel rest, but no abscess or free air.
severity.severe: Complicated by abscess, phlegmon, or localized peritonitis: significant fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, possible ileus or palpable mass; may need percutaneous drainage.
severity.critical: Free perforation with generalized peritonitis and sepsis: diffuse rigidity, hypotension, lactic acidosis; emergency surgery and resuscitation.

red_flags.meaning: Generalized peritonitis from free perforation; urgent surgical evaluation
Sepsis; need immediate resuscitation and source control

red_flags.finding: Persistent or rising fever despite antibiotics
red_flags.meaning: Failed medical therapy; consider abscess or other complication
Large bowel obstruction; may need decompression

complications.name: Bowel obstruction
clues: CT shows dilated colon with transition point

complications.name: Phlegmon
clues: CT shows pericolonic soft tissue stranding without discrete abscess

special_populations.differences: May have milder pain and fever, with only confusion or malaise; higher risk of complications and perforation; need lower threshold for imaging and hospital admission.
Higher risk of severe infection, perforation, and sepsis; localizing signs may be absent; consider broad-spectrum antibiotics and early imaging.
Rare, but gravid uterus may displace sigmoid causing right-sided pain; prefer ultrasound and MRI to avoid radiation; involve obstetrics early.

key_questions.question: Where is the pain, and does it move?
key_questions.looking_for: Left lower quadrant pain that stays there; may be suprapubic but does not migrate to the right lower quadrant

key_questions.question: When did it start, and how has it changed?
key_questions.looking_for: Acute onset over hours to 1-3 days, becoming constant; a slower course can still be diverticulitis

key_questions.question: What makes the pain worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Movement, coughing, deep breathing, or pressure worsening the pain suggests peritoneal irritation

key_questions.question: Any fever or chills?
key_questions.looking_for: Low-grade fever; prominent chills suggest abscess, perforation, or bacteremia

key_questions.question: Any nausea or vomiting?
key_questions.looking_for: Nausea is common; vomiting, when present, usually follows the pain

key_questions.question: Have your bowel habits changed?
key_questions.looking_for: Constipation or diarrhea; obstipation suggests obstruction

key_questions.question: Any burning with urination or blood in the urine?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent or mild; sterile pyuria from adjacent inflammation can mimic a urinary infection

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant?
key_questions.looking_for: Negative pregnancy test in anyone who could be pregnant before ionizing radiation

key_questions.question: Any vaginal discharge or bleeding?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests a gynecologic cause such as pelvic inflammatory disease or ectopic pregnancy

key_questions.question: Have you ever had diverticulosis or diverticulitis?
key_questions.looking_for: Known diverticulosis or prior attacks make diverticulitis much more likely

key_questions.question: Any blood in your stool?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; hematochezia raises concern for diverticular bleed, ischemic colitis, or colorectal cancer

key_questions.question: Any unintentional weight loss?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; weight loss raises concern for colorectal cancer

key_questions.question: Are you taking NSAIDs, steroids, or blood thinners?
key_questions.looking_for: NSAIDs and steroids increase risk and severity of diverticulitis; anticoagulants increase bleeding risk

reasoning_points: Acute left lower quadrant abdominal pain in an older adult
Fever and leukocytosis support an inflammatory process
Localized left lower quadrant tenderness with guarding or rebound
CT shows sigmoid diverticula with wall thickening and pericolonic fat stranding
Look-alikes such as appendicitis, urinary tract infection, and gynecologic disease excluded by history and exam
No free air, abscess, or other complication in uncomplicated cases
Risk factors such as older age, low-fiber diet, or prior diverticulosis

easy: Older adult with classic left lower quadrant pain and low-grade fever
CT shows uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis with pericolonic fat stranding
medium: Patient under 50 with subtle symptoms and a normal white count
Predominant urinary symptoms from adjacent bladder irritation
Pain in the right lower quadrant or suprapubic area from a redundant sigmoid colon
Pregnant patient requiring ultrasound or MRI instead of CT
hard: Older adult with confusion and vague abdominal discomfort but no localizing signs
Immunocompromised patient with severe sepsis and acute abdomen
Free perforation with generalized peritonitis and shock
Diverticulitis plus a possible colonic mass on CT requiring post-recovery colonoscopy
